questions.title: Muscle of mastication responsible for mandibular protrusion
questions.question: Which of the following muscles of mastication is primarily responsible for the protrusion of the mandible?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The masseter elevates the mandible (closes the jaw) via its attachment from the zygomatic arch to the ramus and angle — it is a powerful elevator, not a protrusor.
explanations.B: Correct. The lateral pterygoid is the principal protrusor of the mandible: acting bilaterally, its inferior head (arising from the lateral pterygoid plate) pulls the mandibular condyle and articular disc forward, out of the mandibular fossa and onto the articular eminence — the movement that opens the jaw and juts the chin forward. Acting alone, one side's lateral pterygoid instead produces the side-to-side grinding motion of chewing, making it the only muscle of mastication that pulls the mandible forward rather than closing it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Temporalis elevates and retracts the mandible — its posterior, near-horizontal fibres pull the jaw backward, the opposite action to protrusion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Buccinator is a muscle of facial expression, not mastication — it compresses the cheek against the teeth (as in whistling or blowing) and plays no role in moving the mandible at the TMJ.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the lateral pterygoid as the muscle of mastication that protrudes the mandible, distinct from the elevators (masseter, temporalis) and buccinator.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer 'Lateral pterygoid', FOMSCU Foundation 2 QBank

questions.title: Muscle of mastication responsible for mandibular retraction
questions.question: Which of the following muscles of mastication is responsible for the retraction of the mandible?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Medial pterygoid works with masseter as a sling around the angle of the mandible to elevate the jaw, and it also assists mild protrusion — it does not pull the mandible backward.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lateral pterygoid is the protrudor of the mandible (pulling the condyle forward), the opposite direction to retraction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Masseter's fibres run from the zygomatic arch down to the ramus and angle, so its main action is elevation (jaw closing), with only a minor retraction component compared to temporalis.
explanations.D: Correct. Temporalis is a broad fan-shaped muscle whose fibres converge from the temporal fossa onto the coronoid process; its anterior, near-vertical fibres are the primary elevators of the mandible, while its posterior, more horizontally oriented fibres are what retract the mandible — pulling the protruded jaw back into its resting position. This dual-direction fibre arrangement is exactly why temporalis, uniquely among the muscles of mastication, is credited with both elevation and retraction.

questions.learning_objective: State that temporalis's posterior fibres retract the mandible, distinguishing this from lateral pterygoid's protrusion and masseter/medial pterygoid's elevation.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer 'Temporalis muscle', FOMSCU Foundation 2 QBank

questions.title: Insertion site of the masseter muscle
questions.question: The masseter muscle primarily inserts into which part of the mandible?

options.C: Lateral surface of the ramus and angle

explanations.A: Incorrect. The coronoid process is temporalis's insertion site, not masseter's — the two elevator muscles insert on opposite processes/surfaces of the mandible.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The medial surface of the ramus (and angle) is where the medial pterygoid inserts — masseter and medial pterygoid form a muscular "sling" around the angle, one on the lateral surface and one on the medial, not both on the same side.
explanations.C: Correct. The masseter arises from the zygomatic arch and passes down to insert onto the lateral surface of the ramus and the angle of the mandible. This lateral, external position — easily palpable when clenching the jaw — is what lets masseter act as a powerful elevator, and it is the mirror image of medial pterygoid's insertion on the ramus and angle's medial (internal) surface, the two together forming the sling that suspends and elevates the mandible.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The neck of the mandible is where the lateral pterygoid inserts (onto the pterygoid fovea just below the condyle) — a different site again from masseter's ramus/angle insertion.

questions.learning_objective: State that masseter inserts on the lateral surface of the ramus and angle of the mandible, mirroring medial pterygoid's insertion on the medial surface.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer 'Lateral surface of the ramus and angle', FOMSCU Foundation 2 QBank

questions.title: Insertion site of the medial pterygoid muscle
questions.question: What is the insertion site of the medial pterygoid muscle?

options.A: Lateral surface of the mandibular ramus
options.C: Medial surface of the mandibular angle

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lateral surface of the ramus is masseter's insertion — the two muscles form a sling on opposite surfaces, not the same one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The coronoid process receives temporalis's insertion, a different elevator muscle from a different fossa (the temporal fossa, versus medial pterygoid's origin from the pterygoid fossa).
explanations.C: Correct. The medial pterygoid arises from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate (and a small slip from the maxillary tuberosity) and passes down and laterally to insert onto the medial surface of the mandibular ramus and angle. Together with masseter — inserting on the ramus and angle's lateral surface — medial pterygoid forms a muscular sling that elevates the mandible from both sides at once, and this same muscle also gives a minor assist to protrusion when acting with lateral pterygoid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The neck of the mandible, just below the condyle, is lateral pterygoid's insertion site (via the pterygoid fovea), not medial pterygoid's.

questions.learning_objective: State that medial pterygoid inserts on the medial surface of the mandibular ramus and angle, forming an elevator sling with masseter on the lateral surface.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer 'Medial surface of the mandibular angle', FOMSCU Foundation 2 QBank

questions.title: Muscle responsible for elevating the eyebrows
questions.question: Which of the following muscles is responsible for elevating the eyebrows?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Orbicularis oculi is the sphincter muscle that closes the eyelids (as in blinking or squeezing the eyes shut) — its action lowers, not raises, the eyebrows and eyelids.
explanations.B: Correct. Frontalis is the frontal belly of the occipitofrontalis muscle, a muscle of facial expression that runs vertically in the forehead with no bony attachment inferiorly — instead, it inserts into the skin of the eyebrows and the epicranial aponeurosis superiorly. When it contracts, it pulls the scalp forward and elevates the eyebrows, producing horizontal forehead wrinkles (the look of surprise); this is precisely the muscle Botox commonly targets to smooth those forehead lines.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Orbicularis oris is the sphincter muscle that closes and purses the lips — it has nothing to do with eyebrow position.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Temporalis is a muscle of mastication (it elevates and retracts the mandible), not a muscle of facial expression, and plays no role in eyebrow movement — a homonym-style trap based on both muscles sitting near the temple region.

questions.learning_objective: Identify frontalis as the muscle that elevates the eyebrows, distinct from the sphincter muscles orbicularis oculi/oris and the masticatory muscle temporalis.

questions.title: Location of the submandibular fossa
questions.question: The submandibular gland is located in the submandibular fossa, which is found on the:

options.B: Inferior surface of the zygomatic bone

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lateral surface of the mandibular body is a smooth external surface facing the cheek — it carries the mental foramen but not the submandibular fossa.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The zygomatic bone forms the cheek prominence and part of the orbital rim; it plays no part in housing the submandibular gland, which sits at the mandible, well below the zygomatic region.
explanations.C: Correct. The submandibular fossa is a shallow depression on the medial (inner) surface of the body of the mandible, below the mylohyoid line, and it is exactly where the submandibular gland's larger, superficial part is lodged — the gland wraps around the posterior free edge of mylohyoid, with its smaller deep part continuing above the muscle. The mylohyoid line itself is the key landmark: structures above it (sublingual fossa/gland) sit in the floor of the mouth proper, while structures below it (submandibular fossa/gland) sit in the neck, outside the oral cavity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior surface of the maxilla (the infratemporal surface) faces the pterygopalatine and infratemporal fossae in the upper jaw — an entirely different bone and region from the mandible's submandibular fossa.

questions.learning_objective: Locate the submandibular fossa on the medial surface of the mandible, below the mylohyoid line, as the bed of the submandibular gland's superficial part.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer 'Medial surface of the mandible', FOMSCU Foundation 2 QBank

questions.title: Bony landmark midway between lambda and foramen magnum
questions.question: Which of the following bony landmarks lies midway between the lambda and the foramen magnum?

options.B: External occipital crest and nuchal lines
options.C: Glabella prominence of the frontal bone
options.D: Nasion point of the nasal bones

explanations.A: Correct. The external occipital protuberance (inion) is a palpable bony prominence on the midline of the occipital bone's external surface, positioned midway between the lambda (the suture point where the two parietal bones meet the occipital bone above) and the foramen magnum below. It is a key surface landmark for locating the confluence of the venous sinuses on the internal surface directly opposite it, and it also gives attachment to the ligamentum nuchae and trapezius muscle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The external occipital crest and the superior/inferior nuchal lines radiate out from the external occipital protuberance itself — they are landmarks that extend from this point, not the midpoint landmark being described.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The glabella is a smooth elevation on the frontal bone between the eyebrows, at the front of the skull — nowhere near the lambda-to-foramen-magnum axis at the back of the skull.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The nasion is the midline point where the two nasal bones meet the frontal bone, again at the front of the skull, unrelated to the posterior lambda-foramen magnum landmark.

questions.learning_objective: Locate the external occipital protuberance midway between lambda and the foramen magnum, distinct from anterior skull landmarks (glabella, nasion).

field_notes.keySource: printed answer 'External occipital protuberance', FOMSCU Foundation 2 QBank

questions.title: Bony elevation between the superciliary arches
questions.question: What is the name of the bony elevation located between the two superciliary arches above the root of the nasal bone?

explanations.A: Correct. The glabella is a smooth, slightly raised area of the frontal bone, situated on the midline directly between the two superciliary arches (the brow ridges above each eyebrow) and just above the root of the nose. It is a standard cephalometric and forensic landmark, used as a reference point for measuring facial proportions and for orienting the skull in the standard anatomical (Frankfurt) plane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The nasion sits just below the glabella, at the point where the two nasal bones meet the frontal bone at the root of the nose — the next landmark down, not the elevation between the brow ridges itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The inion is another name for the external occipital protuberance, at the back of the skull — the opposite end of the head from the glabella.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The vertex is the highest point of the skull, on the midline of the calvaria (roof) — a completely different location from the brow-ridge glabella.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the glabella as the frontal bone elevation between the superciliary arches, distinct from nasion (below it), inion (posterior skull) and vertex (skull roof).

questions.title: Ophthalmic artery branch supplying the anterior scalp
questions.question: Which of the following arteries is a direct branch of the ophthalmic artery and supplies the anterior part of the scalp?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The occipital artery is a branch of the external carotid artery that supplies the back (occipital region) of the scalp — the opposite end of the head from the anterior scalp, and not an ophthalmic-artery branch.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The superficial temporal artery, the terminal branch of the external carotid artery, supplies the lateral scalp above the ear — again arising from the external, not internal, carotid system (the ophthalmic artery is a branch of the internal carotid).
explanations.C: Correct. The supraorbital artery is a direct branch of the ophthalmic artery — itself a branch of the internal carotid artery — which it gives off inside the orbit before the ophthalmic artery continues on to supply the eyeball and surrounding structures. The supraorbital artery exits the orbit through the supraorbital notch or foramen, alongside the supraorbital nerve, and ascends onto the forehead to supply the anterior scalp, making it one of the few scalp vessels that ultimately traces back to the internal, not external, carotid circulation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior auricular artery, a small branch of the external carotid artery, supplies the scalp behind and above the ear — a posterior-lateral territory, not the ophthalmic artery's anterior one.

questions.subtopic: Head and neck: scalp arterial supply
questions.learning_objective: State that the supraorbital artery, a branch of the ophthalmic (internal carotid) artery, supplies the anterior scalp, distinct from the external-carotid-derived occipital, superficial temporal, and posterior auricular arteries.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer 'Supraorbital artery', FOMSCU Foundation 2 QBank

questions.title: Nerve supplying sensation to the anterior scalp
questions.question: Which of the following nerves provides sensory innervation primarily to the anterior part of the scalp?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The vagus nerve (CN X) supplies motor and parasympathetic fibres to the thorax and abdomen and a small sensory patch around the external ear — it carries no sensory supply to the scalp.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The facial nerve (CN VII) is predominantly motor, supplying the muscles of facial expression (including frontalis); its sensory component is limited to taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not general sensation of the scalp skin.
explanations.C: Correct. The anterior scalp — from the forehead back to roughly the vertex — is supplied by sensory branches of the ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) divisions of the trigeminal nerve (CN V): specifically the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves (from V1) anteriorly. This is distinct from the posterior scalp, which is instead supplied by cervical spinal nerves (the greater and lesser occipital nerves) — a common exam split between anterior scalp (trigeminal, cranial) and posterior scalp (cervical) sensory territory.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies sensation to the posterior third of the tongue, the pharynx and the middle ear — no scalp territory at all.

questions.subtopic: Head and neck: scalp sensory innervation
questions.learning_objective: State that the trigeminal nerve (V1/V2 branches) supplies the anterior scalp, distinct from the posterior scalp's cervical (occipital nerve) supply, and from the vagus, facial and glossopharyngeal nerves' own territories.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer 'Trigeminal nerve', FOMSCU Foundation 2 QBank

questions.title: Nerve carrying pain sensation from the cheek
questions.question: An emergency physician used local anesthesia for surgery to drain an abscess affecting the cheek area. Which of the following nerves must be anesthetized because it carries pain sensation from the cheek area?

options.A: Buccal branch of the facial nerve
options.B: Buccal branch of the mandibular nerve

explanations.A: Incorrect. The buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) is a motor branch that supplies the buccinator and other muscles of facial expression around the cheek and mouth — it carries no sensory (pain) fibres at all, a classic confusion the near-identical name is designed to test.
explanations.B: Correct. The buccal nerve (long buccal nerve) is a sensory branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve, arising from the anterior trunk of V3. It passes forward between the two heads of the lateral pterygoid to reach and supply general sensation — including pain — to the skin and mucous membrane of the cheek and the buccal (cheek-side) gingiva of the mandibular molars, which is exactly the territory an abscess of the cheek would need blocked for pain-free drainage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The inferior alveolar nerve, also a V3 branch, supplies sensation to the mandibular teeth and the skin of the chin and lower lip via the mental nerve — a different sensory territory from the cheek itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lingual nerve, another V3 branch, supplies general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and the floor of the mouth — again a different territory from the cheek.

questions.subtopic: Head and neck: trigeminal sensory branches
questions.learning_objective: Identify the buccal branch of the mandibular nerve (V3) as the sensory supply to the cheek, distinct from the motor buccal branch of the facial nerve and from the inferior alveolar/lingual nerves' own territories.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer 'Buccal branch of the mandibular nerve', FOMSCU Foundation 2 QBank

questions.title: Muscle classified as strap-like
questions.question: Which of the following muscles is anatomically classified as a strap-like muscle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The deltoid is a multipennate muscle, with fibres converging from three distinct heads (anterior, middle, posterior) toward a single tendon — a fan-like arrangement, not a long parallel strap.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rectus abdominis is a flat muscle interrupted by tendinous intersections, giving it a segmented rather than a single unbroken strap shape.
explanations.C: Correct. The sartorius is the longest muscle in the body and is architecturally classified as a strap muscle: a long, narrow, ribbon-like muscle whose fibres run largely parallel to each other along its whole length, from its origin at the anterior superior iliac spine to its insertion at the pes anserinus on the medial tibia. This parallel-fibre, uniform strap shape (as opposed to a fusiform, pennate or fan-shaped architecture) is what earns sartorius the classification, and it also explains its distinctive spiral course across the front and medial side of the thigh.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Biceps brachii is a fusiform (spindle-shaped) muscle — broad in its belly and tapering at both ends into tendons — a different architecture from the uniform-width strap muscle.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the sartorius as a strap muscle (long, parallel-fibred), distinct from multipennate (deltoid), segmented (rectus abdominis), and fusiform (biceps brachii) architectures.

questions.title: Joint type at the epiphyseal growth plate
questions.question: What kind of joint is typically seen in the epiphyseal growth plate of a long bone?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fibrous suture joints are the immobile joints of the skull vault, joined by fibrous tissue with no cartilage involved — an entirely different joint class from the growth plate.
explanations.B: Correct. Primary cartilaginous joints are hyaline and temporary — bones united by hyaline cartilage, and the epiphyseal (growth) plate is the textbook example: it is the hyaline cartilage plate between the epiphysis and diaphysis of a growing long bone, permitting longitudinal bone growth, and it is temporary because it eventually ossifies and fuses once growth is complete (the epiphyseal line). Secondary cartilaginous joints, by contrast, are fibrocartilaginous and midline (like the pubic symphysis or intervertebral discs), and are permanent structures rather than temporary growth sites.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Secondary cartilaginous joints are fibrocartilaginous and midline, permanent structures (e.g. pubic symphysis, intervertebral discs) — not the hyaline, temporary growth-plate joint being described.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Synovial plane joints are freely mobile joints with a joint cavity and synovial fluid (e.g. the acromioclavicular joint) — the growth plate has no joint cavity and is not freely mobile at all.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the epiphyseal growth plate as a primary (hyaline, temporary) cartilaginous joint, distinct from secondary cartilaginous, fibrous suture, and synovial joints.
